title: Plants that reliably deposit durable additional carbon in soil

concept.text: The proposed innovation is plants whose inherited traits reliably increase the amount of atmospheric carbon retained in soil for a defined, long period while preserving useful crop productivity. Plants capture carbon through photosynthesis and transfer some of it below ground through roots and their interactions with microbes. The breakthrough would be to control those processes so that improved plants leave additional persistent soil carbon compared with conventional plants grown under comparable conditions. Salk’s documented research strategy explores root depth, root size, suberin and plant–fungus partnerships as possible contributors to this outcome.

Conceptual synthesis: success requires more than moving carbon deeper or producing larger roots. New plant-derived carbon must increase persistent soil carbon after accounting for decomposition, losses of carbon already present, limits on soil storage, cultivation inputs and other greenhouse gases. Additional storage is the increase attributable to the improved plants relative to a credible comparison; durability concerns how long that increase survives. Net climate benefit requires a separate accounting of the emissions and removals associated with achieving and maintaining it.

significance.text: If this capability were reproducible at substantial scale while maintaining productivity, crop breeding could become a means of removing atmospheric carbon on existing farmland. Carbon storage would become an intentionally selected crop function alongside agricultural performance. Salk’s program connects the aspiration for soil carbon storage with productive and resilient crops, but the supplied announcement does not establish that these outcomes have been achieved together.

Conditional impact synthesis: varieties that delivered a verified net benefit could potentially spread through existing seed and farming systems, extending carbon-removal activity across land already used for food production. The eventual climate contribution would depend on removal per unit area, the area suitable for adoption, farmer uptake, persistence, monitoring costs and emissions across the production system. Maintaining productivity would matter both for agricultural viability and for avoiding pressure to replace lost production elsewhere. None of those downstream benefits follows automatically from a favorable root trait.

Impact limits: a larger or deeper root system is a potential mechanism, not a measurement of durable removal. Even increased soil carbon at one sampling depth could represent redistribution rather than a whole-profile gain. Soil storage should therefore not be treated as equivalent to an unlimited or permanently sealed carbon reservoir: the relevant claims must specify how much additional carbon remains, for how long, under which soils and management conditions, and with what net greenhouse-gas balance.

missing_breakthrough.text: The central missing capability in the supplied research program is a reliable connection between controllable plant traits and measured, additional, persistent soil carbon under field conditions. Salk identifies deeper and larger roots, slowly decomposing suberin and plant–fungus partnerships as candidate mechanisms. Its proof-of-concept framing leaves open whether those mechanisms can produce the intended durable storage in practical cropping systems. The supplied evidence does not establish the worldwide state of this problem beyond that program.

Scientific barrier synthesis: plant carbon delivery and soil carbon retention are different processes. More carbon entering soil may decompose, alter microbial activity or coincide with losses of older soil carbon. Root chemistry and placement must therefore work with the local soil and microbial environment to increase retained carbon rather than merely increase carbon turnover. The target also requires understanding where storage capacity becomes limiting and why the same trait may perform differently across soils, climates and management systems.

Engineering and measurement barrier synthesis: the useful traits must remain effective in productive crops across seasons without requiring inputs whose emissions erase the benefit. Measurements must distinguish newly added carbon from existing carbon, changes in total stocks from redistribution, and temporary accumulation from persistence. A practical system also needs defensible estimates of other greenhouse gases, uncertainty, reversal risk, yield and cost. These are requirements of the proposed net-removal target; the supplied announcement does not document their comprehensive assessment.

current_state.text: On September 22, 2026, the Salk Institute announced field evaluation of deeper-rooted soybean lines as its research moved from laboratory discovery toward agricultural testing. The announcement describes extending an ongoing Illinois study and adding Midwest trials, with comparisons between Ideal Soybean varieties and conventional varieties over multiple years. This documents an active comparative research program; it does not report completed demonstrations of additional, durable net carbon removal.

The announcement presents root depth, root size, suberin and plant–fungus partnerships as routes to investigate for durable soil carbon storage. Its removal projections are modeled possibilities conditional on the plants performing as expected in field conditions. They should not be read as measured field removal rates, demonstrated permanence or verified net climate benefits. The supplied research and review do not reproduce numerical projection values, so no quantitative removal estimate can be responsibly carried into this record.

The supplied review reports that the announcement’s retained HTML was complete, matched the intended source and had no reported truncation or extraction problems. The interpretation here rests on that review, rather than a fresh inspection of the document. No bounded freshness search was supplied, so the record cannot establish comprehensive coverage through November 1, 2026 or determine whether subsequent developments changed the picture. This coverage limit does not negate the September announcement.

A PDF retained alongside the announcement was identified in the supplied review as an investigator conflicts-of-interest policy revised August 17, 2026. Although its extraction reportedly included all 15 pages without truncation, it is unrelated to the soybean research and supplies no scientific corroboration. Its presence neither supports nor refutes the field-testing claims.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed demonstration: compare improved plants with matched conventional controls in replicated, multi-year trials spanning contrasting soils and climates. Record baseline conditions and management so that any difference can reasonably be attributed to the plants. Salk’s announced multi-year comparison of Ideal Soybean and conventional varieties provides a relevant starting point, but the broader framework proposed here is not presented as Salk’s published protocol or an established consensus standard.
completion_criteria.label: Replicated multi-year comparisons against conventional controls across contrasting environments

completion_criteria.text: Proposed carbon-accounting demonstration: trace new plant-derived carbon and measure changes in whole-profile soil carbon stocks, using methods that can detect redistribution and losses of existing carbon. Combine those results with measurements or defensible estimates of other greenhouse gases and life-cycle emissions from inputs and operations. A convincing result would show a positive additional net removal with reported uncertainty, rather than relying on root biomass or a carbon increase in a single soil layer.
completion_criteria.label: Positive additional net removal with full emissions accounting and uncertainty

completion_criteria.text: Proposed durability demonstration: define the storage horizon and acceptable uncertainty before evaluating success, then test retention over time and after relevant management changes. Longer observations and validated persistence models could support claims extending beyond the trial period, with their assumptions made explicit. Multi-year trials alone cannot establish indefinite storage, and no particular persistence horizon or numerical success threshold is established by the supplied evidence.
completion_criteria.label: Carbon retention meets predefined storage horizon and uncertainty criteria

completion_criteria.text: Proposed reproducibility and practical boundaries: independent teams should reproduce the net benefit, while evaluating yield, input requirements and cost against suitable controls. Results should identify where the approach works, where it fails and what management it requires. Finite trials can establish demonstrated breadth across tested environments; they cannot prove literal universality across all crops, soils or climates.
completion_criteria.label: Independent reproduction of net benefit with practical operating boundaries

related_concepts.text: Roster-based synthesis: BOT-16, “Predictable control of plant–mycorrhizal nutrient exchange,” has the closest mechanistic overlap because plant–fungus partnerships may influence below-ground carbon allocation and crop nutrition. Predictable nutrient exchange and persistent carbon storage nevertheless have different endpoints. Improved exchange would not by itself demonstrate additional soil carbon or a positive net greenhouse-gas balance.

Roster-based synthesis: BOT-15, “Broadly transferable perennial grain production,” could intersect through longer-lived root systems and different cultivation patterns. BOT-07, “Transferable resurrection-like desiccation tolerance in productive crops,” and BOT-08, “Programmable, durable plant immunity against diverse pathogens,” concern traits that could help crops function under stress. These capabilities could affect the reliability or management of a carbon-storing crop, but perennial growth, survival and immunity each remain distinct from verified durable carbon removal.

Roster-based synthesis: BOT-02, “A functional carbon-concentrating photosynthetic system in rice,” concerns carbon capture during photosynthesis, whereas BOT-10 concerns the additional carbon retained after transfer into soil. BOT-01, “Nitrogen-fixing partnerships for major cereal crops,” could intersect with the input and emissions accounting of a cropping system. Greater photosynthetic capture or altered nitrogen supply would still require separate evidence that whole-system net removal increased.

Roster-based synthesis: BOT-04, “An inexpensive, broadly transferable method to edit and regenerate plants,” could help introduce candidate traits; BOT-05, “Predictive plant biology from genome to whole-organism performance,” could help anticipate their effects. BOT-13, “A predictive mechanism for plant cell-wall growth and mechanical sensing,” could inform root development, while BOT-14, “Programmable, multigenerational epigenetic inheritance of adaptive plant traits,” concerns another route to maintaining traits across generations. These are possible enabling capabilities with their own success criteria. None substitutes for demonstrating persistent additional soil carbon in the field.

unresolved_issues: The supplied evidence does not establish completed measurements of additional persistent soil carbon or comprehensive net greenhouse-gas benefit from the improved soybean lines.
A persistence horizon, minimum useful removal rate, uncertainty requirements and acceptable yield and cost boundaries remain unspecified.
The field performance, soil dependence, storage limits and reversal risks of the proposed traits remain unresolved in the supplied material.
The announcement’s numerical modeled removal projections are not reproduced in the supplied research or review and therefore cannot be preserved quantitatively here.
No bounded freshness search was supplied, so later developments and the broader worldwide state through November 2026 cannot be established.
The intended scientific PDF, if one was expected, remains unidentified; the retained policy PDF cannot fill that evidence role.

brief.title: Crops that keep extra carbon in soil for the long term
possible: Farmers could grow productive crops that take carbon dioxide from the air and leave extra carbon in soil for a defined, long period. Inherited plant traits would increase storage compared with conventional crops grown under comparable conditions.
why: Farmland could help remove carbon from the atmosphere while continuing to produce food. Breeders could select crops for carbon storage alongside agricultural performance, and farmers could adopt them through existing seed and farming systems.

sources.showed: Salk identified candidate genes linked to carbon-storing root traits. It is extending field studies comparing deeper-rooted soybeans with conventional varieties.
sources.quote: That work enabled Salk scientists to identify 347 potential gene candidates tied to carbon-storing root traits
sources.cited_for: Inherited root traits are being developed and tested as a route to greater soil carbon storage.
sources.not_established: The soybean work has not demonstrated additional, lasting soil carbon storage with an overall climate benefit.

sources.showed: Switchgrass varieties differed in fine roots and their effects on soil structure and soil organisms. Those differences did not produce differences in soil carbon after ten years.
sources.quote: However, at present, ten years of cultivation generated no differences in soil C among the studied cultivars.
sources.cited_for: Differences in root traits and soil processes do not necessarily produce greater carbon storage.
sources.not_established: The study did not demonstrate that selecting root traits increases lasting soil carbon storage.

shown: Salk is testing deeper-rooted soybeans against conventional varieties in field studies. Its approach also explores larger roots, partnerships with soil fungi, and suberin, a cork-like root compound that decomposes slowly.

Jin Ho Lee and colleagues found that switchgrass varieties differed in fine roots and soil processes, yet soil carbon did not differ after ten years. Root changes alone have not demonstrated the intended lasting storage.
missing: Field trials have yet to connect the improved soybean traits to reliably greater, lasting soil carbon storage.
Measurements must distinguish new carbon storage from carbon moving between soil layers or replacing older carbon.
The overall climate benefit must account for farming emissions and other greenhouse gases.
Lasting storage must be demonstrated alongside useful crop yields, practical inputs and acceptable costs.

milestones.label: Repeated field comparisons across soils and climates
milestones.explanation: Repeated trials over several years would have to compare improved and conventional plants across contrasting environments, accounting for starting conditions and management. This would establish whether the plants cause the difference.

milestones.label: Extra carbon removal after all emissions are counted
milestones.explanation: Measurements would have to track new carbon, total storage through the soil depth, older carbon losses and farming emissions, with uncertainty reported. This would establish whether the plants deliver an overall climate benefit.

milestones.label: Carbon stays stored for the agreed period
milestones.explanation: Observations and tested models would have to establish retention over a predefined period, including after relevant management changes, within agreed uncertainty. This would distinguish lasting storage from temporary accumulation.

milestones.label: Independent teams reproduce benefits under practical farming conditions
milestones.explanation: Independent teams would have to reproduce the overall climate benefit while comparing yields, inputs and costs with conventional crops. This would establish where the approach works and what management it needs.

uncertain: The required storage period, minimum useful removal and acceptable uncertainty, yield and cost limits remain undefined.
It remains unclear how soil, climate and management affect storage capacity and the risk of releasing stored carbon.

page.title: Crop improvement for soil carbon sequestration
page.definition: Crop varieties whose inherited root traits increase atmospheric carbon retained in soil relative to conventional varieties while maintaining harvested yield. Additional storage remains net positive after greenhouse-gas emissions and carbon re-release are deducted, with retention supported over at least 100 years.

goal.need: A global model, corrected in 2018, estimated that human land use depleted 116 billion metric tonnes of carbon from the upper 2 m of soil relative to a world without agricultural land use. Breeding crops for additional root-derived soil carbon addresses this depleted reservoir; the historical loss does not quantify how much improved crops could restore.

statements.body: The National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine identify high-carbon-input crop phenotypes, with maintained above-ground yields, as a research priority.
statements.quote: Research is needed to develop crop varieties with altered root morphology and biomass

statements.body: The US Department of Energy’s ARPA-E ROOTS programme targets greater carbon deposition depth and accumulation, alongside 50% lower fertilizer nitrous oxide emissions and 25% greater water productivity.
statements.quote: a 50% increase in carbon deposition depth and accumulation
statements.context: ROOTS means Rhizosphere Observations Optimizing Terrestrial Sequestration; this is the ARPA-E programme, distinct from Salk’s later project of the same name.

statements.body: The Salk Institute’s Harnessing Plants Initiative sets increased root-carbon storage lasting centuries as its objective.
statements.quote: store larger amounts of carbon from the atmosphere in their roots and keep it buried in the ground for hundreds of years.

completion.title: An improved crop delivers additional net soil-carbon storage for 100 years without yield loss.
completion.criterion: Under comparable field conditions, inherited crop-root traits produce additional atmospheric CO₂ removal into soil, with harvested yield at least equal to conventional varieties. Independent assessment supports positive net storage for at least 100 years after life-cycle greenhouse-gas emissions, leakage and expected carbon re-release are deducted. Measurements and a justified durability assessment support the storage horizon; 100 years of direct observation is not required. No minimum removal rate or planted area is added.
completion.set_by: Atlas synthesis of Salk’s yield goal and XPRIZE’s durability criterion; neither body published this combined crop-genotype test.
completion.basis: Searched Salk HPI goals and field-testing plans, ARPA-E ROOTS, XPRIZE Carbon Removal rules and Verra VM0042; no genotype-specific completion test combines additional soil carbon, net emissions, durability and maintained yield. This synthesis uses XPRIZE’s 100-year net-storage criterion and Salk’s current-crop yield floor, without adding a removal-rate threshold.

milestones.title: A crop variety expresses its selected root trait in growth-chamber and greenhouse tests.
milestones.criterion: Candidate genes produce the intended change in root depth, root biomass or suberin, a root-barrier polymer, during crop phenotyping. Salk’s published sequence tests gene effects in growth chambers and advances selected lines to greenhouses under varied soil and climate conditions. In 2025 Salk reported 38 engineered lines across five crop species; this developer report is not peer reviewed and does not give numbers passing each stage.
milestones.set_by: Salk Institute, HPI development sequence published in Inside Salk, Spring 2025; written for Salk crop lines.
milestones.threshold_quote: evaluate whether each candidate gene is producing the desired trait.

milestones.title: A root-trait crop matches or exceeds the harvested yield of conventional varieties.
milestones.criterion: A root-trait crop meets Salk’s goal of yield at least equal to current crops. The published goal supplies no statistical equivalence margin or required number of seasons. Rice entered a field trial in Colombia in autumn 2024; soybean field comparisons were announced on 22 September 2026. These developer announcements are not peer reviewed and do not report completed yield comparisons.
milestones.set_by: Salk Institute, HPI’s published crop-yield acceptance goal in its Frequently Asked Questions.
milestones.threshold_quote: One of HPI’s fundamental goals is producing plants that will equal, if not exceed, the yields of current crops.

milestones.title: An improved crop stores more soil carbon than conventional varieties over multiple years.
milestones.criterion: Comparative field results show greater soil-carbon storage under the improved crop over multiple years. Salk announced this soybean test on 22 September 2026, without reporting its endpoint. For switchgrass, six cultivars in four replicated blocks showed root-trait differences but no cultivar differences in soil carbon concentration at 5–10 cm depth after ten years, sampled in October 2019. That result does not test whole-profile stocks.
milestones.set_by: Salk Institute, ROOTS field-testing plan of 22 September 2026; the published comparison is for soybean.
milestones.threshold_quote: test whether Salk Ideal Soybean varieties can store more carbon than conventional varieties over multiple years.

milestones.title: A crop-root intervention achieves positive annual net CO₂ removal on a life-cycle basis.
milestones.criterion: Life-cycle assessment establishes positive annual net CO₂ removal attributable to the crop-root intervention after associated greenhouse-gas emissions and leakage are deducted. This is XPRIZE’s annual net-negative-performance component. Durability is tested at completion.
milestones.set_by: XPRIZE Foundation, Carbon Removal Guidelines version 2.2, page 17, Net Negative Performance; general criterion covering agricultural solutions.
milestones.threshold_quote: Teams must demonstrate using a Lifecycle Analysis that their solution results in net CO₂ removal (“negative emissions”) on a lifecycle basis annually

not_found: No published crop-genotype-specific test combining net removal, a storage horizon and maintained yield was found in the searched programmes and standards.
No registered Salk soybean protocol specifying replication, sampling depth, statistical endpoints and a durability-validation test was located.
No cited field result establishes annual net removal and the combined completion criterion for soybean, rice or switchgrass.

results.finding: Six switchgrass cultivars showed no differences in soil carbon after 10 years.
results.detail: The field experiment used four replicated blocks. Soil carbon was measured at 5–10 cm depth, so the result does not assess whole-profile carbon stocks. Limited statistical power may have obscured small differences.
results.quote: However, at present, ten years of cultivation generated no differences in soil C among the studied cultivars.

results.finding: Transgenic soybean lines, sample size not stated, showed up to 1.3-fold greater root fresh/dry weight.
results.detail: Plants were maintained in growth chambers and greenhouses, but the text does not identify where the reported root measurements were taken or establish expression in both settings.
results.quote:
Under non-stress conditions,
GmNAC19-
and
GmGRAB1-
overexpressing plants had up to 1.7-fold increase in root length and/or 1.3-fold increase in root fresh/dry weight.

results.finding: Two OsMYB92a-overexpressing rice lines, with 6 plants per line, formed root suberin lamellae 5 mm from the apex.
results.detail: The selected root trait was observed in seedlings, but the supplied text does not establish testing in both a growth chamber and a greenhouse.
results.quote: These transgenic seedlings formed both a lignin-based broad band and SL at the endodermis in the region 5 mm from the root apex, a pattern similar to that observed in the region 30 mm from the WT root apex

results.finding: Three PvNHX1-overexpressing switchgrass lines had 1.55-fold greater root fresh weight than wild-type plants.
results.detail: Plants were grown in a greenhouse. The paper does not report growth-chamber tests or identify increased root biomass as a selected trait.
results.quote:
As shown in Fig. 1c
and d , root fresh weight and shoot dry weight in the
transgenic lines were 1.55-fold and 1.46-fold, respect-
ively, greater than in the corresponding tissues of WT

results.finding: Deep-rooting Dro1-NIL rice, with 3 replications per treatment, yielded approximately 10% more grain than conventional IR64.
results.detail: The comparison used an irrigated paddy field at one location over two years, with and without fertilizer. The study did not measure soil carbon retention.
results.quote: At maturity, Dro1-NIL showed approximately 10% higher grain yield than IR64, irrespective of fertilizer treatment.

results.finding: Dimorphic-root rice, 20 plots per genotype, yielded 22% more grain than IR64.
results.detail: The 2024 comparison covered five fertilized and unfertilized environments in Madagascar. The study did not assess soil carbon retention.
results.quote:
The grain yield of
DRO1
+
qsor1
-PYL was 22% higher than that of IR64.

results.finding: Transgenic switchgrass, sample size not stated, produced up to 160% more aboveground biomass than wild-type controls.
results.detail: Greenhouse-grown plants had significantly greater root and aboveground biomass; the best line was compared with wild-type controls.
results.quote: A significant increase in both aboveground and root biomass was observed in transgenic greenhouse grown plants compared to wild-type control plants with the best line producing 160% more aboveground biomass than controls.

results.finding: Perennial rice, three soil-sampling replicates: soil organic carbon increased by 0.95 Mg ha−1 yr−1 over four years.
results.detail: Soil was sampled under perennial and annual rice, but the supplied text does not state the annual-rice carbon result or quantify a difference between systems. Perennial rice was not tilled between harvests, while annual rice was ploughed and replanted.
results.quote:
In the 0–40 cm soil layer, PR cropping 
over four years resulted in increased soil organic carbon (SOC) and 
total nitrogen (TN) at rates of 0.95 and 0.11 Mg ha−1 yr−1, respectively 
(Fig. 3b, Extended Data Fig. 8 and Supplementary Table 9).

results.finding: Six switchgrass cultivars differed in bulk soil carbon concentration by 40% at 0–10 cm.
results.detail: Cultivars were grown for 27 months. The abstract reports soil carbon concentrations, not whole-profile stocks, and does not identify an improved cultivar or a conventional comparator.
results.quote: bulk soil C concentrations beneath switchgrass cultivars varied by 40% in the 0–10 cm soil depth and by 70% in the 10–20 cm soil depth
